1135.title: Why leave your home
1135.hook: the yogis catch the traveler who praises staying, and ask why he left home
1135.howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's long journeys as the udasis, and read this exchange in the Sidh Gosht as his own account of why he traveled: to seek the Gurmukhs and share the Name.

segments.voice: Yesterday Nanak answered with a duck in the stream, and your line was the duck stays dry. Today the yogis spot a problem with that answer.

Fair point, the yogis might say. You tell us to stay in the stream, work, keep a home. So what are you doing up here? The man praising the household life is standing on a mountain, far from his own household, dressed for the road. In the Sidh Gosht they put it to him directly. Why did you leave your home and become a wanderer, an udasi? Why take on this way of dressing? What are you trading in, and how will you carry anyone across? It's the sharpest question yet, because it's about him.
screen: `YOU PRAISE STAYING.` → `SO WHY ARE YOU HERE?` → `THE YOGIS ASK THE TRAVELER.`

segments.voice: Nanak's answer, in paraphrase: searching for the Gurmukhs, I became a wanderer. I took on this way of dressing for the sake of a glimpse of the One. I'm a trader in the merchandise of truth. And through the Guru, a person crosses over and carries others across. Piece by piece. First, he went looking for people: Gurmukhs, those whose faces are turned toward the Guru. Not a place, not a secret, not a technique; people who live facing the good. In his telling, he didn't go out to get away from the world. He went out to find the best of it. Second, the clothes. He doesn't claim his road clothes make him holy. They serve the looking, the longing for a glimpse; the outfit is for the journey, not the point of it. Third, the trade. A trader goes from town to town, buying here, selling there. Nanak takes that picture for himself. What he carries is truth, and the deal is that it gets passed on. So the traveling doesn't contradict the duck. The duck was never told to sit still; it swims. Tradition says Nanak's journeys ended at Kartarpur, where he settled, farmed and kept a household, with people coming to him. The road was for seeking and sharing; home was where it was lived. And the question doesn't offend him. They catch him in what looks like a contradiction, and he simply tells them why.
screen: `SEARCHING FOR THE GURMUKHS.` · `THE ROAD CLOTHES SERVE THE LONGING.` · `A TRADER IN TRUTH.` · `THE ROAD SEEKS; HOME LIVES IT.` · then, large: `SEEKING THE GOOD.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone you've met who lives facing the good, kind without fuss, honest when it costs something, and let their face come clearly. What's one good thing you picked up from them, a habit, a sentence, a way of treating people? Hold it for a few breaths, the way a trader holds something worth carrying, and if you pray, give thanks for the person you pictured.
Why leave your home. The yogis' question to the traveler, and Nanak's answer: searching for the Gurmukhs, and trading in truth. Today's word.
Your line: seeking the good. A trader in truth carries it on. Thanks for sitting with me.

1136.title: The yogis' earrings
1136.hook: the yogis offer Nanak their earrings, bag and patched coat; he names what he'd wear instead
1136.howItsDone: Sikhs do not take on the yogis' earrings or patched coat; the Sidh Gosht's answer is read as moving those outward marks inward, and some keep a line of Gurbani in mind through the day as a way of wearing the Word.

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked why Nanak left home, and your line was seeking the good.

A ring through the ear is hard to take off. The yogis Nanak met wore earrings as a mark of their order, and tradition says the ring marked an initiation, a road a person had chosen for good. Add a shoulder bag and a coat stitched together from patches, and the look was unmistakable. In the Sidh Gosht they make Nanak an offer: take on our look, our earrings, our bag, our patched coat. Join us.
screen: `A RING THAT DOESN'T COME OFF.` → `EARRINGS, BAG, PATCHED COAT.` → `JOIN US, THEY SAY.`

segments.voice: It's a generous offer, made with pride: our path is the best of the yogic paths, the yogis say, in paraphrase. Nanak doesn't mock the earrings. He takes each piece and moves it inside. His answer, in paraphrase: let the Word, the shabad, be the earring, worn within, never taken out. Clear away ego and the grip of mine. Let go of lust, anger and pride, and through the Guru's Word, real understanding comes. And for the patched coat and the bag: see the Lord filling everything. The One, Nanak says, carries a person across. Look at what he kept. He kept the idea of the earring: something worn always, a mark of who you belong to, a sign you aren't going back. He just put it where nobody can see it. The yogi's ring is in the ear; Nanak's is in what the ear keeps hearing. The coat too. The yogi's coat is made of scraps sewn together. Nanak's is the whole world, with the One stitched through every piece. There's an echo from the Japji, where he gave the yogis earrings of contentment. Here, the earring is the Word itself. Think about what an earring does all day. You forget it's there. Then you catch it in a mirror, or it brushes your neck when you turn your head, and you remember. That's one way to picture what the stanza asks of the Word: a line of Gurbani that keeps catching the light through an ordinary day, bringing you back.

segments.voice: Choose one short line you've met on this path, a line of Gurbani, the word Waheguru, or today's line itself, and imagine fastening it in place the way you'd put on an earring in the morning. Then let it go quiet, and every few breaths let it catch the light again; if the mind wanders, that's fine, since an earring is easy to forget, and each time you notice, you've found it again. If you pray, the line you chose can be the prayer, worn quietly.

1137.title: Where did it begin
1137.hook: the yogis ask about the very beginning, and Nanak answers with wonder
1137.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of bismaad, wonder or awe, as a fitting response to the Creator and creation, and the Sidh Gosht's answer about the beginning is read in katha alongside the Japji's opening and the hymns of the time before creation.

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis offered their earrings, and your line was the word as earring. Today the questions get bigger.

What was there before there was anything? Small children ask it at bedtime, usually right after the light goes off. Physicists ask it with chalk. And in the Sidh Gosht, the yogis ask it of Nanak. So far they've asked about him: who he is, how he lives, why he travels, what he wears. Now they ask about everything. What can you say about the beginning? Before anything was made, where was the void, the sunn, at home?
screen: `BEFORE THERE WAS ANYTHING?` → `THE YOGIS ASK ABOUT EVERYTHING.` → `WHERE WAS THE VOID AT HOME?`

segments.voice: The heart of Nanak's answer, in paraphrase: of the beginning, all one can speak of is wonder. The One dwelt then in itself, in the void, without end. The word for wonder is bismaad, the word Sikhs use for awe so large it leaves you without anything to add. Notice what Nanak doesn't do. He doesn't hand the yogis a list of steps, first this, then that. He gives no date and no mechanism. Asked the biggest question there is, he gives a one-word answer: wonder. That's not a refusal. It's a report. In this poem, the beginning is met with astonishment, not with a diagram. Then he takes the yogis' own word, sunn, the void, and doesn't argue with it; the word belonged to their own practice. He agrees there was a void before all things. He just says who was there: the One, dwelling in itself. The emptiness wasn't empty. Near the start of the Japji there's a similar move: the One before the ages, true in the beginning. And elsewhere the Guru Granth Sahib speaks of a long darkness before creation, where only the divine order was. The texts don't try to make the beginning ordinary. They let it stay huge. The coffee, the birdsong, the fact that there's anything at all instead of nothing: in this poem, the right first response to all of it is bismaad.
screen: `OF THE BEGINNING: ONLY WONDER.` · `BISMAAD, AWE WITHOUT WORDS.` · `NO STEPS, NO DATE, NO MECHANISM.` · `THE VOID WASN'T EMPTY.` · then, large: `IT BEGAN IN WONDER.`

segments.voice: Choose one ordinary thing within reach of your senses, your own hand, the light in the room, a sound outside, and look or listen as if it had only just appeared, letting the question come gently: why is this here at all, instead of nothing? Don't try to answer, since Nanak didn't give the yogis a mechanism either; when the mind starts explaining, just come back to looking. If you pray, let that astonishment be the prayer, without words.
Where did it begin. The yogis' question about the beginning, and Nanak's answer: of that, one can only speak with wonder, and the One dwelt in the void. Today's word.
Your line: it began in wonder. Not with a diagram, but with astonishment. See you tomorrow.

1138.title: Where does the mind live
1138.hook: the yogis ask where the restless mind dwells, and Nanak says the Word steadies it
1138.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of steadying the mind through simran and through listening to and singing Gurbani, returning attention to the Word rather than relying on the yogic postures the Siddhs practiced.

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked about the beginning, and your line was it began in wonder. Today the question comes closer: not the universe, the mind.

A body can sit in one chair for an hour. In a single minute of that hour, a mind can visit an email, a worry about money, a song from years ago and the question of dinner. It gets around. The yogis worked hard at holding the mind still. So in the Sidh Gosht they ask Nanak about it. Where does this mind live? Where does it rest, and how is it held?
screen: `THE BODY IS IN A CHAIR.` → `THE MIND IS EVERYWHERE.` → `WHERE DOES IT LIVE?`

segments.voice: Nanak's answer, in paraphrase: the mind finds its place through the Guru's Word. Without the Word it wanders; with it, the mind settles and comes home to itself. Gurbani has a phrase for that home, nij ghar, one's own house, the place inside where a person is finally at rest. Take that apart. First, the question assumes the mind has an address, and Nanak doesn't dispute it. The mind does have a home. The trouble is that it keeps leaving. Second, what steadies it. The yogis had tools for holding the mind: postures, breath, long hours of discipline. The anchor Nanak names is the shabad, the Word, the hymns of the Guru the mind can return to. That's a practical answer. You can't always hold a posture. You can always come back to a line. Third, the verb. The Word doesn't trap the mind or beat it into silence. It steadies it, the way a hand on a wobbling table steadies it. The table is still a table; it just stops rocking. So the mind here isn't an enemy. It's a resident who keeps wandering off, and the Word is the familiar voice that calls it back inside. And the poem keeps this inside the same life as the duck in the stream. The steadying doesn't wait for a mountain. It happens in traffic, at the desk, at two in the morning, whenever the mind comes back to the Word.

segments.voice: Choose one line, a line of Gurbani you know, the word Waheguru, or simply today's line, and say it once, quietly or inside. Then let the mind do what minds do, and each time you notice it has wandered off, to the inbox or the dinner or the old song, don't scold it; just say the line again, like a hand on the table, counting the returns if it helps, since the coming back is the practice. If you pray, the line itself can be your prayer.

1139.title: The Word is the Guru
1139.hook: the yogis ask who Nanak's guru is, and he answers: the Word is the Guru, attention is the disciple
1139.howItsDone: Sikhs honor the Guru Granth Sahib as the living Guru, bowing before it in the gurdwara, and often cite 'sabad guroo surat dhun chelaa' when explaining why the Word, not a human lineage, is the Guru.

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked where the mind lives, and your line was the word steadies. Today they ask whose Word it is.

Who did you study with? Ask a classical musician and you'll often hear a name, and behind that name another, a line of teachers going back through the years. In that world, your teacher is part of who you are. The yogis Nanak met also spoke of teachers and their disciples. So, in the Sidh Gosht, they ask the obvious question. What is the root of all this? Who is your guru? Whose disciple are you?
screen: `WHO DID YOU STUDY WITH?` → `A LINE OF TEACHERS.` → `WHO IS YOUR GURU, NANAK?`

segments.voice: Here a few of the original words are worth hearing: sabad guroo, surat dhun chelaa. Sabad is the Word, the shabad. Guroo, the Guru. Surat is attention, awareness. Dhun is the tune, the strain of the music. Chelaa is the disciple. So, in paraphrase: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. He goes on: speaking the unspoken, he stays unattached, and through all the ages, the Lord of the world is his Guru. Look at what he doesn't say. He gives no human name, no line of teachers to check. The yogis asked for a person, and he gives them a relationship. On one side, the Word. On the other, your own attention, tuned to it, the way a string is tuned to a note. A guru, in this answer, isn't someone you trace back. It's something you listen to now. And the disciple isn't a body sitting at someone's feet; it's the part of you that pays attention. So anyone who listens can be a disciple, today, wherever they are. The teaching reaches whoever tunes in. It also explains something about Sikh life. Sikhs today bow before the Guru Granth Sahib, a book of hymns, as the Guru. A visitor seeing that for the first time may be surprised. In this stanza, Guru Nanak had already answered the yogis that way: the Word is the Guru.

segments.voice: If you can, play a shabad you love, quietly, or let one line of Gurbani you know sit in the silence, or simply Waheguru, and be the disciple in the stanza: not a body at someone's feet, just attention resting on the sound the way a string settles on a note. When it drifts, that's the string going slack; bring it gently back into tune, without trying to understand every word. If you pray, the listening itself can be the prayer.

1140.title: Crossing the ocean
1140.hook: the world is an ocean hard to cross; Nanak says attention on the Word carries you over
1140.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the world as bhav saagar, the world-ocean, and of the Guru's Word and the Name as what carries a person across; the image returns in Gurbani sung in kirtan.

segments.voice: Yesterday the yogis asked who Nanak's guru was, and your line was the word is guru.

Dutar. Hard to cross. That's how the yogi Charpat describes the world when he puts his question to Nanak, near the start of the Sidh Gosht. The world is an ocean, he says, and they call it hard to cross. How does anyone reach the far shore? Six days ago came half the answer, the duck that swims the stream and stays dry. But the duck was only the first move, and the stanza doesn't leave Charpat in the water.
screen: `DUTAR: HARD TO CROSS.` → `CHARPAT'S OCEAN.` → `THE DUCK WAS HALF THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: The rest of the stanza, in paraphrase: with attention fixed on the Word, the terrifying world-ocean is crossed by speaking the Name. The phrase for the world-ocean is bhav saagar. Saagar is the sea. Bhav is the world of becoming, the churn of being born, wanting, losing, wanting again. Nanak accepts the yogi's picture. He doesn't say the world is a calm pond or that Charpat exaggerates. The water really is deep, and the waves are real. What he changes is the way across. One way is to climb above the water, onto a peak the waves can't reach. Nanak's answer goes through it: attention resting on the Word holds a person up while they cross. Elsewhere in the Guru Granth Sahib, the Guru and the Name are pictured as a boat or a ship. The world is the ocean; the Word is the boat. And the picture is honest. A boat doesn't make the sea smaller. The storm still comes, and you still get wet. But a person in a boat isn't fighting the water with their own arms; they're held by something built for the crossing. Yesterday, attention tuned to the Word was the disciple. Today, it's how the disciple crosses: learning, and staying afloat. On a bad night, one line, held, may be all a person has, and in this stanza it carries someone over.
screen: `BHAV SAAGAR: THE WORLD-OCEAN.` · `NANAK ACCEPTS THE DEEP WATER.` · `ATTENTION ON THE WORD CARRIES.` · `THE BOAT DOESN'T SHRINK THE SEA.` · then, large: `THE WORD IS THE BOAT.`

segments.voice: Let your eyes rest on some water, a glass on the table, rain on a window, or just the memory of a lake, and let the breath come and go like small waves. Bring to mind one thing that feels deep or rough right now, and without trying to calm it, picture yourself held above it, giving your attention one line to rest on: Waheguru, or today's line, the word is the boat. If you pray, let that line carry the weight for a while.
Crossing the ocean. Charpat's question about the world-ocean, hard to cross, and Nanak's answer: with attention on the Word, a person crosses over. Today's word.
Your line: the word is the boat. It doesn't shrink the sea; it carries you across. Thanks for sitting with me today.

1141.title: Without the Guru
1141.hook: line after line, the Sidh Gosht says what is missed without the True Guru
1141.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of the need for the Guru, the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib, as the guide to the Name, and the Sidh Gosht's lines on life without the True Guru are sung and explained in kirtan and katha.

segments.voice: Yesterday Charpat asked how to cross the world-ocean, and your line was the word is the boat. Today, near the poem's end, a run of lines.

On a mountain trail, what matters can be tiny: a stripe of paint on a tree, a little pile of stones at a fork. Someone walked this way before you and left a sign. Without it, the trail splits, the light goes, and every path looks the same. The yogis in the Sidh Gosht had their own teachers. Near the poem's end, Nanak speaks to exactly that, in lines that each begin the same way: without the True Guru.
screen: `A STRIPE OF PAINT ON A TREE.` → `SOMEONE WALKED HERE FIRST.` → `WITHOUT THE TRUE GURU…`

segments.voice: Here are those lines, in paraphrase. Without serving the True Guru, there is no real yoga. Without meeting the True Guru, no one is set free. Without meeting the True Guru, the Name can't be found. Without the True Guru, a person suffers deeply, lost in the dark of pride. And without the Guru, Nanak says, a person loses the game of life. The repetition is the point, like someone tapping the same spot on the map: here, here, here. The yogis already had teachers, so the surprise isn't that a guide is needed. It's what this poem has said the Guru is. Two days ago, asked who his guru was, Nanak answered: the Word is the Guru, and attention tuned to it is the disciple. So, read inside the Sidh Gosht, without the Guru means without that Word to steer by. Sikhs honor the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib as the Guru, the one light carrying that Word. And look how the week has built. Why leave home? To seek the Gurmukhs. The earrings? The Word, worn within. Where it all began? In wonder. Where the mind lives? The Word steadies it. Who his guru was? The Word. How to cross the ocean? Attention on the Word. Every answer has pointed the same way, and today's lines say plainly why. In this poem, nobody finds that way alone. The stripe of paint on the tree isn't an insult to the hiker. It's a gift from someone who went first.
screen: `WITHOUT THE TRUE GURU: NO WAY.` · `THE REPETITION IS THE POINT.` · `IN THIS POEM, THE GURU IS THE WORD.` · `EVERY ANSWER POINTED ONE WAY.` · then, large: `A GUIDE IS NEEDED.`

segments.voice: Let someone come to mind who showed you the way at a fork in your life, a teacher, a grandparent, a friend, an author, a stranger who said one right thing at the right time, and stay with their face, or the page, or the moment, for a few breaths. Notice where you might be without that stripe of paint, and silently thank them. If you pray, say Waheguru on each slow breath, in thanks for every guide.

Your line: a guide is needed. In this poem, the guide is the Word. A week on the mountain, done.
